---
title: "Python matrix tests and vanilla STACK"
subtitle: "How the port can extend vanilla STACK without disguising the difference"
---

## Why add a basis test?

A basis is a set of building blocks for a vector space. Its vectors must belong
to that space, be independent, and span the whole space. There is usually no
single correct list of vectors. Multiplying a vector by a nonzero number,
changing the order, or taking suitable combinations can produce another basis.

`AlgEquiv` compares matrices by dimensions and corresponding entries. That is
appropriate when a question asks for a particular matrix. It would reject many
correct answers to “give any basis.” `IsBasis` asks a different mathematical
question: **do these vectors form a basis for the same space as the reference?**

The [worked questions](../examples.qmd#matrix-problems-from-ingmat-3a) adapt
Andrey Chesnokov's INGMat 3A exercises. For the matrix

$$C=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&6\end{pmatrix},$$

the null-space equation is $z_1+2z_2+3z_3=0$. A reference basis is

$$T=\begin{pmatrix}-2&-3\\1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$

The columns $(-5,1,1)$ and $(-1,-1,1)$ also give a correct basis: both satisfy
the equation and they are independent. Their entries do not match $T$, which
is why this exercise needs a basis test rather than `AlgEquiv`.

## How this extends vanilla STACK

This is an intentional addition to the Python port, not a newly implemented
native STACK answer test. A familiar file format need not mean an identical
set of mathematical capabilities.

| Part of the question | What happens here | Relationship to vanilla STACK |
|---|---|---|
| Question text, variables, inputs and PRTs | A Moodle-style STACK XML question describes the activity | The existing structure is retained |
| `AlgEquiv` | Compares a matrix with its expected entries | An existing native answer-test name and compatibility target |
| `MatrixProperty` | Tests exact integer-entry, determinant or identity conditions | A new Python-only name; three PRTs retain the determinant example’s three-part grading |
| `IsBasis` | A registered Python function checks a submitted basis against a reference space | A new Python-only answer-test name; the XML requires this port |
| Resizable matrix dimensions | The learner chooses the number of columns within author bounds | The explicit `<matrix>` configuration is also a port extension |
| True/false response-tree branches | The chosen branch awards the authored score and feedback | The existing PRT mechanism is retained |
| Vector colors | The helper explains membership and dependence | Optional presentation supplied by this implementation; it does not set scores |

The `IsBasis` and `MatrixProperty` files are therefore **STACK-style XML for this Python port**, not
drop-in vanilla STACK exports. Native STACK does not gain the Python checker by
importing the XML. A native implementation would need an equivalent custom
Maxima checker, together with compatible input configuration. The ordinary
rank/pivot example uses native answer-test names, but its resizable input
configuration still needs adapting for a native installation.

This is a small example of how the port could develop its own Python features
while continuing to read existing STACK questions. It does not rename or fork
the project, or change the meaning of an existing native answer test. The
official native compliance inventory and its supported scope remain unchanged;
the new examples and tests provide separate evidence for the Python extension.

## What the XML says

The question author supplies one known basis as the teacher answer. With vectors
in columns, a node looks like this:

```xml
<node>
  <name>0</name>
  <answertest>IsBasis</answertest>
  <sans>ans</sans>
  <tans>T</tans>
  <testoptions>columns</testoptions>
  <truescoremode>=</truescoremode><truescore>1</truescore>
  <truenextnode>-1</truenextnode><trueanswernote>basis-T</trueanswernote>
  <falsescoremode>=</falsescoremode><falsescore>0</falsescore>
  <falsenextnode>-1</falsenextnode><falseanswernote>basis-F</falseanswernote>
</node>
```

`ans` must name a matrix input directly. `T` must evaluate to an independent,
nonempty reference basis. `columns` is the default; `rows` selects vectors
stored in rows. These are fixed option names, not executable expressions.

**The reference defines the target space.** `IsBasis` does not independently
discover that it is a null space. The author must verify that $T$ is a basis
for the space named in the prompt. The input’s own teacher answer must itself pass `IsBasis` against the reference;
otherwise the build fails. This catches wrong model answers and input shapes
that would make a correct basis impossible. Our example tests independently verify
$BT=0$ or $CT=0$ and the expected dimensions. Giving the wrong reference would
define the wrong target even if the checker itself worked perfectly.

The test checks whether each nonzero submitted vector lies in the reference
span and whether the submitted family is independent and complete. Permuting,
rescaling or mixing vectors is allowed whenever these conditions still hold.
Zero vectors, vectors outside the space, repeated/dependent vectors and
incomplete families do not pass.

`IsBasis` returns a true/false decision to the PRT. It does not bypass its
branches. The reused helper also computes a fractional diagnostic score, but
this port deliberately does **not** turn that number into partial credit. The
examples award one point for a complete basis and zero otherwise. This is a
documented change from the source math-exercise checkers.

## Where the Python functionality lives

The reusable `assess_basis` function comes from a pinned revision of
`Erasmus-CTM/math-exercise`. Its function body is copied unchanged into
`stack_sympy/basis_helper.py`, with the required imports added. The
[provenance record](../questions/course-examples-provenance.json) identifies the
course exercises; the helper's source revision, source hash, extracted-function
hash, module hash and AGPL license are recorded separately in
`vendor/basis-helper-provenance.json`. No upstream math-exercise refactor is
needed for this extraction.

`stack_sympy/python_tests.py` supplies the bounded adapter and registers the
names `IsBasis` and `MatrixProperty`. XML selects that reviewed function by name. It cannot supply
Python source, choose imports or name arbitrary modules. Adding another Python
test means adding reviewed code and tests to the registry; this is not a
general-purpose Python execution field in XML.

The same Python modules are bundled into the browser worker and used by local
CPython. The UI does not contain a second mathematical checker. Validation
checks syntax, dimensions and the allowed numeric domain; it does not disclose
whether the vectors are a basis. Grading runs the PRT and then displays the
helper's feedback and vector colors. Quiet PRT nodes suppress that diagnostic
feedback and coloring.

## What the colors mean

| Color | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Green | This nonzero vector belongs to the space, and the complete locally valid submitted family is independent |
| Yellow | This nonzero vector belongs to the space, but the locally valid family is dependent; every member of that family is yellow |
| Red | This vector is zero or outside the target space |

Green is not a promise that the whole answer is complete. For example, one
valid column in a two-dimensional space is green but cannot form a basis of
the whole space. With dependent columns, no vector is singled out just because
it was entered last. Invalid vectors remain red while dependence is assessed
among the valid ones. Text feedback accompanies the colors.

Editing, resizing, resetting or changing variants clears the assessment and
requires validation again. These colors explain a checked answer; they never
award cell, row or column credit on their own.

## Present limits and evidence

The first version supports exact rational entries, written as integers or
fractions with bounded arithmetic. Decimals, symbolic parameters, irrational and complex entries are
rejected. Each rational numerator and denominator is limited to 256 bits.
Every arithmetic step is bounded before the general evaluator runs; nested
powers cannot construct arbitrarily large integers before rejection. Scalar
function calls are outside this extension’s arithmetic grammar, even when a
function could simplify to a rational value. Existing native scalar tests keep
their own syntax and semantics.

Existing matrix limits also apply: 1–16 rows and columns, at most 64 entries,
and the bounded input grammar. These limits keep rank and membership checks
exact and predictable rather than relying on numerical tolerances.

The matrix editor currently requires positive dimensions. An empty basis for
the zero space is therefore outside this first `IsBasis` input contract,
although the underlying general helper understands empty families. Neither
example asks for an empty basis.

Authored XML tests include different correct bases and wrong, dependent,
incomplete and zero submissions. Unit tests also cover row orientation,
invalid references, bounds, input validation and PRT behavior. Browser tests
exercise the actual worker, column colors, stale-result clearing and reset.
These checks establish the Python behavior; they are not native STACK parity
results for `IsBasis`.

## MatrixProperty: preserve a custom exercise’s three conditions

The determinant-one activity comes from math-exercise’s
`custom-special-linear-matrix` example. It asks for an integer $2\times2$
matrix with determinant 1, different from the identity. A single model answer
is not enough: many different matrices satisfy those constraints.

`MatrixProperty` exposes a small, reviewed vocabulary of exact checks:

| `testoptions` | Teacher answer (`tans`) | What is compared |
|---|---|---|
| `integer_entries` | `true` or `false` | Whether every entry is an integer |
| `determinant` | An exact rational number | The determinant of a square matrix |
| `identity` | `true` or `false` | Whether the matrix is square and equal to the identity |

The source checker gave one third for integer entries, one third for determinant
1, and one third for being different from the identity. The XML adaptation
retains that policy using three equally weighted PRTs with teacher values
`true`, `1`, and `false`. Each PRT uses an ordinary true/false branch. For example,
the identity earns two thirds but not full credit; a rational noninteger matrix
with determinant 1 can also earn two thirds. The feedback identifies which
condition still needs work. There is no inferred per-cell partial credit.

This differs from the binary IsBasis examples: the property exercise awards
credit for separate authored requirements, while each basis exercise asks for
a complete basis. Both scoring policies are visible in the XML. Neither is
invented by the matrix editor.

Like IsBasis, MatrixProperty is Python-only. Native STACK authors could compute
these properties with appropriate Maxima expressions and build equivalent PRTs,
but importing this XML alone does not install a new native answer test. The
input model answer must satisfy every MatrixProperty node too. General matrix
arithmetic remains outside the expression parser; these registered checks do
not enable arbitrary matrix code in question variables or learner input.
